clue.text: Anatomically does it tend to cause a stiff neck ?

definitions.text: Anatomically does it tend to cause a stiff neck ?

parts.words: Anatomically does it tend to cause a stiff neck ?
parts.note: read as a collar with a stiffening bone in it, the thing that makes a neck stiff, while anatomically it is a real bone near the neck

explanation.surface: A medical question about what gives people a stiff neck.
explanation.walkthrough: Old shirt collars were stiffened with bones, so a collar bone would make the neck stiff; 'Anatomically' points to the real bone at the base of the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The clavicle is the bone running from shoulder to breastbone, just below the neck.

parts.note: headgear tops a head as a mortarboard tops a scholar, and peaked headgear is worn outdoors in the sun

explanation.surface: An exclamation about things picking up a suntan on deck.
explanation.walkthrough: The grid as filed has CABS, an OCR slip: 10 Across is PENNY (Hamlet's 'truepenny'), so the third letter is P.
explanation.definitionFit: Hats with peaks top the head, as a mortarboard tops an academic.

clue.text: No sea burial for this old German

parts.note: land is the opposite of sea
a grave is a burial place

explanation.surface: An old German is buried on shore rather than at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a burial custom; read literally, 'No sea' is the opposite of sea and 'burial' its plot, and a landgrave was a German count.
explanation.definitionFit: A landgrave was a count with territorial jurisdiction in the Holy Roman Empire.

definitions.meaning: read literally, any road will do

explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means regardless, and literally it says whichever road is taken.

clue.text: Does she 'show Ireland a dance first ?

definitions.text: Does she 'show Ireland a dance first ?

indicators.note: first says the dance comes before the other pieces

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a dancer gives an Irish audience a dance before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' says the dance comes before Ireland and 'a'; read whole, the clue also pictures a dancer performing.
explanation.definitionFit: A female classical dancer performs in shows, sometimes on tour abroad.

indicators.note: among means the letter for love goes inside the word for the sisters

parts.note: nuns are religious sisters
O is love, a zero score in tennis

explanation.surface: Affectionate language heard in a convent.
explanation.definitionFit: Naming words such as table or dog are a class of words.

parts.note: a means one
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of the British police

explanation.surface: A police force is put through an examination.
explanation.walkthrough: Gold was proved by touching it with nitric acid, hence the acid test.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid is the reagent of the classic assay for gold, so the word serves as a test.

clue.text: Nerissa disguised as one of Trollope's trio

definitions.meaning: in The Merchant of Venice Nerissa dresses as a lawyer's assistant

explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Nerissa poses as an office assistant, and Trollope's novel has three such men.

clue.text: They make up in the prescribed manner

definitions.text: They make up in the prescribed manner

parts.words: They make up in the prescribed manner
parts.note: make up suggests cosmetics, but means preparing medicines as a doctor's prescription directs

explanation.surface: People applying make-up by the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Pharmacists prepare medicines following a doctor's prescription.

parts.note: a movement forward never goes back, though backing also suggests support

explanation.surface: A political movement without supporters.
explanation.definitionFit: A forward move is the opposite of retreat.

clue.text: True value of the Ghost in Hamlet

definitions.text: True value of the Ghost in Hamlet

parts.words: True value of the Ghost in Hamlet
parts.note: Hamlet calls his father's ghost ... ('Art thou there, ...?...), so the Ghost's 'true' value is a coin

explanation.surface: A literary question about what the Ghost really means in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The grid as filed has BENNY, an OCR slip for PENNY: Hamlet's nickname for the Ghost is 'truepenny', and the crossing 1 Down is CAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: In Act 1 Hamlet addresses the spirit as 'truepenny', making the coin its value.

clue.text: Might she be described as a clean-living person ?

definitions.text: Might she be described as a clean-living person ?

parts.words: Might she be described as a clean-living person ?
parts.note: clean-living is read literally: a woman who earns her living by cleaning clothes

explanation.surface: A question about whether a woman leads a virtuous life.
explanation.definitionFit: A washerwoman makes her living by washing linen, so her living is literally clean.

clue.text: 23, but not on the distaff side

definitions.text: 23, but not on the distaff side

parts.words: 23, but not on the distaff side
parts.note: 23 Across is RELATED; the distaff side is the female line, so this is kinship through the father

explanation.surface: Kinship that excludes the female line.
explanation.walkthrough: The distaff (a spinning stick) stands for women, so 'not on the distaff side' means through males.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnatic kin are relatives descended through the male line from a common forefather.

parts.note: read as one bond (a fetter), worn by a chained prisoner, rather than fashion from the London shopping street

explanation.surface: A question about fashionable clothes from Bond Street, the smart London shopping street.
explanation.walkthrough: Bond Street is an expensive London shopping street; split, 'Bond' is a fetter and 'Singular' says one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A fetter is a single iron ring or chain binding a prisoner, a bond worn on the leg.

clue.text: It indicates that I am omitted from "Who's Who "!

definitions.text: It indicates that I am omitted from "Who's Who "!

parts.words: It indicates that I am omitted from "Who's Who "!
parts.note: read not as a complaint about the reference book but as the mark in Who's replacing the letter i of who is

explanation.surface: A complaint about being left out of the reference book of notable people.
explanation.walkthrough: Who's Who is a British directory of notable people; 'I am omitted' is the letter I of 'is' dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: The raised comma shows a letter dropped, as in a contracted 'is'.

definitions.meaning: an old verb for growing thin and sickly, to pine

explanation.definitionFit: To pine and grow sickly is the old verb sense, and a summit is the everyday noun.

clue.text: To which strikers resort to settle their disputes

definitions.text: To which strikers resort to settle their disputes

parts.words: To which strikers resort to settle their disputes
parts.note: strikers suggests workers in an industrial dispute, but here they are people throwing punches

explanation.surface: Workers on strike turning to some method of settling a dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: A fight with bare hands is how hitters settle a quarrel.

indicators.note: re-sort means sort again, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A holiday spot for reckless Scotsmen.
explanation.walkthrough: Re-sort RASH SCOTS; the result is a wooded glen near Loch Katrine, a Scottish beauty spot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trossachs are a wooded Scottish glen popular with tourists since Scott's day.

clue.text: Here the box-office receipts are evidently nil

definitions.text: Here the box-office receipts are evidently nil

parts.words: Here the box-office receipts are evidently nil
parts.note: box-office suggests boxing promotion; a bout for which nothing is charged

explanation.surface: A show that earned nothing at the box office.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl in which anyone may join, with no admission charge implied.

parts.note: the theatre screen that falls when a performance is over

explanation.surface: The close of a game.
explanation.definitionFit: The drop of the stage cloth marks the close of a theatrical performance.

clue.text: Direction to embezzler, who looks for a profit

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south, a compass direction
a peculator is one who embezzles public money

explanation.surface: Advice for a fraudster on how to turn a profit.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who buys shares or goods in hope of a rise in price is out for gain.

definitions.meaning: a drop of liquid from the eye
a rent is a rip in cloth

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a droplet from a weeping eye, the other a rip in fabric.

definitions.note: the clue gives an adverb; the answer is a noun, the state of someone acting unconsciously

indicators.note: break means the word canter is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A horse moving into a canter without thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' looks like the start of 'break into a canter'; it is the anagram signal on CANTER, and 'into a' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypnotic state in which a person acts without awareness.

definitions.note: the clue's telling is the act of narrating; the answer is the matching past participle, narrated

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape anew, so the letters of the clue word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something changed in a striking way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion' is the anagram signal, turning ALTERED into the answer; 'telling' is the definition, in the sense of recounting a story.
explanation.definitionFit: To relate a story is to recount or narrate it.

parts.note: in the Odyssey and Tennyson, the ...-eaters eat a fruit that makes them forget and idle

explanation.surface: Something to eat for lazy people.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit of the lotus-eaters brought dreamy forgetfulness.

clue.text: Red in Worcestershire, and follows the hounds in London

definitions.text: Red in Worcestershire, and follows the hounds in London

parts.words: Red in Worcestershire, and follows the hounds in London
parts.note: ... is a town in Worcestershire and ... a street in London; the same word follows Red and Hounds

explanation.surface: A fox-hunting scene in two English places.
explanation.walkthrough: Redditch is a Worcestershire town; Houndsditch is a street in the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The trench word ends both place names, Redditch and Houndsditch.

parts.note: an exclamation at cheek or nerve, but read as a part of the neck, its nape

explanation.surface: An exclamation at someone's impudence.
explanation.definitionFit: The back of the neck, by which a cat or a culprit is grabbed.

clue.text: Stupefy in the most un likely way

indicators.note: in says the letters are found inside the following words

explanation.surface: Amazing someone in an improbable manner.
explanation.definitionFit: To daze or knock senseless.

parts.note: a lover of the countryside need not be a lover of his nation, though the phrase can mean both

explanation.surface: A remark that a lover of rural life need not hold some quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Loving one's nation is what this adjective describes, distinct from enjoying rural life.

parts.note: Tennyson's poem Maud has the line 'the black bat, ..., has flown'

explanation.surface: A creature from a Victorian poem.
explanation.definitionFit: In Maud the poet calls the dark hours a black bat that has flown away.

parts.note: a middy is a midshipman; Captain Marryat's novel Mr Midshipman ... put one in a book

explanation.surface: A young naval officer being punished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought to book' usually means punished; here it means put into a novel, Marryat's Mr Midshipman Easy.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Marryat's fictional midshipman hero, Jack.

clue.text: The author has not returned to the city

parts.note: Chester is a cathedral city in Cheshire, England

indicators.note: returned means the word not is turned round and written backwards

explanation.surface: A writer has not gone back to town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns 'not' backwards, and 'to the city' says that reversed word is joined onto the city's name.
explanation.definitionFit: G. K. Chesterton was an English writer, creator of Father Brown.
